utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please remember that you are under solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you were saying very fairly that it's nearly nine years since you were there and that your memory for names has faded. This doesn't involve names, but I was wondering if during your period of six months where you were carrying out intelligence reconnaissance, did you come across the existence of any not quite military units, in other words, not attached to the army, called independent military units or anti-terrorist groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, at least for the time being. It's very difficult to think back. At the time, it was difficult to tell a regular unit from another unit which was not regular, because everything was moving. Everything was developing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I appreciate that you said that there was an air of irregularity about most affairs there at the time you were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irregularity, but it proceeded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter did not understand. Could --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irregularity permeated the whole atmosphere of the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. I think your answer is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I have said this applies to both groups, both factions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Both factions. I appreciate that. And I appreciate that you said that everybody who had a gun considered himself a policeman --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: -- and everybody seemed to be wearing some kind of a uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But you didn't come across any independently financed or private groups or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS JJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have access to that type of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge Clark's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I do not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, thank you very much for helping us by giving your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will take you out of the room. We also would like to thank the Spanish interpreters for your valuable help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender the following documents: Exhibit 325, 352, 375, 361, 363, 374, 383 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would Mr. Prosecutor perhaps go through those one more time. The very first four, five, or six I didn't catch. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: After this sitting, you might provide us with a list listing all those numbers so that we could, you know, have a clear picture of the whole documents you are going to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. I've got. But I should make one remark, then, because Exhibit 2 is also indicated on this list, but it has already been tendered through Jan Van Hecke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Then my second remark will be that actually most of the mentioned documents have already been tendered through Jan Van Hecke, but so far we don't have any decision, whether positive or negative, if the documents have been accepted. So -- but we have also three documents. This is Exhibits 508, 595.1, 612, that have never been tendered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that this time, you only have to tender those that haven't been tendered before, because we already have the record of the previous documents tendered by Mr. Van Hecke during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I would like to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please repeat all those numbers once again, because both the Madam Registrar and the Defence counsel have some difficulty to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. 325, 352, 357, 361, 363, 374, 383, 385, 401, 405, 407, 423, 461, 474, 476, 502, 508, 523, 538, 570, 595.1, 612. All these documents have been examined during my direct examination and redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Some of these documents, it is correct, we have addressed in an earlier motion, and some were tendered through Mr. Van Hecke. I see now that through this witness, there has been further foundation laid; however, this is, again, a batch of documents coming in. We would request the time to specifically raise objections to the documents that we will object to further, and with further grounds for the objections. There are some documents that this witness just testified, JJ, that he could vouch for the high credibility of those. Others, he could not. So we would ask for the 30 days. My next concern, Your Honours, is very important. And that is, because of a prior ruling of this Trial Chamber that all documents to be introduced against our clients would be rendered in a language of their native tongue, a language they can understand and read, none of these documents have been so interpreted into the language that we -- our client can read, understand, to try to help in his own defence and let us know his thoughts. So that's a problem. That's a concern we, again, raise. We would, again, ask for the 30 days, because it's a batch of documents. And I understand, Your Honours, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber's ruling, if it's an individual document, we have seven days. Once we can sit down and review these documents with the testimony of JJ, we will then, within the previous order of the Court, the 30-day time period, in writing, tell the Trial Chamber which documents we object to and which ones we do not. Whichever ones we do not object to or whichever ones the Trial Chamber in its wisdom determines should be admissible, we would just remind and ask the Trial Chamber to accept those and give them whatever weight you feel necessary given the testimony of JJ and the credibility of the various documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in our part of the case, we shall set out to prove that most of these documents have no probative value, and we shall be in a position to know more about that when we consult our client after all these documents are translated. So at this particular point in time, do I not have any objection to the production of these -- to the tendering of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott. Are you going to inform us about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to address, Your Honour, several outstanding document-related issues. I think the time has come when we must clarify some situations here, because I do -- I do have concerns, on behalf of the Prosecution, as to where we are going with this. Let me be clear. Before the trial started, we provided to the Defence and to the Chamber approximately 17 binders of documents. This is now going on two months ago. There should be no question or doubt it is our view and it is our plan before the Prosecution case is over to tender virtually all of those documents, and in fact, a substantial number of them have now -- by now have been tendered. Substantially more, if we have time, will be tendered in the next -- today, perhaps and in the next couple of days. There should be no question about that, and the Defence should not have any different understanding. They will have to review and should be -- have been in the process of reviewing the 17 binders, which that is one of the reasons they were provided to them approximately two months ago. We are concerned about the rulings on the exhibits in the case. We appreciate the fact that there are a large number of documents. However, I think the Chamber -- I hope the Chamber will understand that we will not be in a position to rest the Prosecution case until there is a final ruling on the Prosecution exhibits. Let me give the Chamber an example of that. If whatever reason the Chamber were to come back and say that some particular documents lacked foundation, we would certainly seek a further opportunity to address that and to provide the Chamber with additional foundations for documents. We certainly -- we can't be in a position to do that until the Chamber has expressed at least its preliminary ruling. We are at a point in the case -- we hope to finish the Prosecution case, with a little bit of luck and good fortune, we would like -- hope to finish the Prosecution case by the 11th of December. Now, it only takes fairly short math that that is just about 30 days from now. So if the situation is that the Defence is given 30 days to respond, we will quickly be at a point where they will not be responding until after the Prosecution has finished its case. And then that puts us in a bind, Your Honour. So I'm just telling the Chamber, the Prosecution will not be in a position to rest its case, and subject to the court orders, we will not rest our case until there is a final ruling on all the exhibits so that we have a fair opportunity to respond to any deficiencies perceived by the Chamber in the documents. Concerning the translations, Your Honour, we are very aware of the Chamber's ruling. Quite candidly - I don't think I'm giving away any big secrets if I say this - we were quite surprised by the Chamber's ruling. We believe it's a completely -- changes the rules of the game contrary to the practices of the Tribunal, after the game, might I add, had already started. This had never been required before. It had never been required during the pre-trial phases of the case when Judge Wald was the Pre-Trial Judge. So we are doing our best that we can to respond. It may be months before those translations are available. It's our prediction that there are some perhaps 1.000 pages that will require translation. The Translation Unit tells me that one translator can be -- can do approximately five pages a day. Now, obviously we have to compete with every other case. There are other cases set to commence trial in the next few weeks and months. The Galic case begins very soon. They have a large number of documents with translations outstanding. The Milosevic cases have a large number of documents. Every case, every case has a large number of documents outstanding. So it's not just the Tuta and Stela case. I have asked the Translation Unit to give our documents as much priority as they can, but we compete with very, very limited translation resources to obtain these translations. I have asked the Translation Unit to give me an estimate of when they believe all of these documents could be translated. So far, they have not given me a response, but it's easy to see that it could easily take several months for these translations to be provided. That's the situation we're in, Your Honour. Again, we're doing our best to respond to the Court's ruling. And the Court's ruling was that any documents tendered after the 17th - I'll get my date's straight here - the 12th of November would have to be tendered together with the B/C/S translation. The Chamber's ruling did not establish that requirement prior to the 12th of November, and to respond to some of the comments that the counsel has made just now, we have not been required up to this point in time to tender our documents with the B/C/S translations in place. So that's not been a requirement, and we have not done so, except that we have undertaken steps to have the translations made as quickly as possible. I'll be happy to provide the Chamber with my correspondence to the Translation Unit if that will assist you, but so far they have not given me any prediction as to when they can finish. There's approximately 312 documents that have to be translated, comprising at least, at least a thousand pages of documents, perhaps quite -- perhaps substantially more. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I sit here and I listen to my colleague Mr. Scott basically complain about this Trial Chamber's previous ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I take it back. His concerns. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Meek. Mr. President, you were consulting with Judge Clark. I want this to be very clear. I object strongly to that characterisation. I did not complain about the Chamber's ruling. I did express candidly and I think with respect the concerns raised and that we are taking every step possible to address the Chamber's ruling. But it is unfair to say that I am complaining about the Chamber's ruling. I have not done so. I have candidly advised the Chamber of the situation that we find ourselves in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, let me hear what Mr. Meek is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I certainly apologise to Mr. Scott. He is raising concerns now over a ruling that the Trial Chamber made some weeks ago. He has been in this Tribunal longer than any of us, and he understands the rules. If he did not like the Trial Chamber's ruling, he had a right to ask for an interlocutory appeal. He did not do that. Apparently, it's my understanding from reading cases, there is no such practice as a motion to reconsider. I understand the problems that the Prosecutor is confronted with; but frankly, when it comes to problems that the Prosecution office is confronted with when weighed against the right to a fundamentally fair trial to these accused who stand accused of very serious war crimes by definition or they would not be sitting in this Trial Chamber today, I think that the concern is minimal. I also see that the Trial Chamber made a ruling that documents tendered after the 12th of November which allows a window of opportunity for the Prosecution to come in before that time and tender massive amounts of documents so that they do not have to be translated, thereby skirting the intentions, the good intentions and good ruling, this Trial Chamber made in regards to translation of documents. And that's the position we find ourselves in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. After hearing from the -- yes, Mr. Seric. I'm sorry, I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I should like to refer to what you said on the 18th of October this year, Mr. President, when you said that correctness should take precedence over efficiency. We have that recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seric, for reminding me of what I have said. I think up to now we are facing some problems with the documents. We understand after about five weeks' sitting, there are piles of documents waiting for a decision before this Trial Chamber. And this Trial Chamber had a meeting yesterday concerning the admission of all the documents, and we will make some decisions about some of the documents that were tendered by the Prosecutor in the past few weeks. As for the documents tendered today by the Prosecutor, I think only three documents that are new, and the others were already tendered by Mr. Van Hecke during his testimony. And those three documents, namely, 508, 595.1, 612, are not so complicated documents. We would like to know whether these three documents have their B/C/S translations at this stage. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will check it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will check it, Your Honour. At least, yes, one of these documents has been translated into B/C/S, and I will give you the number of this document. Yes, this is Exhibit 595.1. And I would add that 59 documents, SpaBat documents, had been submitted to the Defence before in B/C/S translation. It was made on our own initiative, when we had some time and the translation unit had some time. So it was our pleasure, maybe, at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So as for those documents that have been translated into B/C/S, namely, the three documents, Mr. Meek, I don't believe you will have 30 days to submit your response. We will give you seven days for these three documents for your response. And this Trial Chamber will soon make decisions concerning all the documents tendered by the Prosecutor. And also, this Chamber has some questions to ask. Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think I must confess that the reason why there has been such a delay in a decision in relation to the documents on my difficulties, which have been attributed to the background that I come from, not dissimilar to yours, my difficulties in appreciating what exactly this Trial Chamber means by the "word" tender. It apparently has a different meaning in The Hague to the ordinary English meaning. But the difficulty I have that's arising now is a new difficulty. On the first few days of the trial, in fact, it might have been the first and second day of the trial, because I was just scanning the transcript yesterday, there was an objection made to the furnishing of those 17 binders on the Defence within a relatively short period before the trial commenced. And my understanding of the debate which took place was that you said -- maybe I led you to say that -- but you said that those documents, binders, the documents in the binders were being proffered, as a neutral word, to the Court and to the Defence to ease the trial, to oil the wheels of the trial so that if a document was called for which would become an exhibit, that we would have access to them. I understood that they were the Prosecution's response to the failure -- or maybe that's too strong a word -- the choice, the choice that the Defence made not to seek disclosure, and that they were disclosure. Am I correct in understanding you now to say that, in fact, those documents are now all going to become exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me try to give a full response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you understand where I'm coming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do. As I say, let me try to give as full a response to Your Honour as I can. I agree with Your Honour completely that I think the two of us share, certainly not an identical legal background, but I think a quite similar one. And admittedly, the way that some documents and exhibits are handled at the Tribunal, I suspect, are different than they are in Ireland and in the United States. But that is one of the cultural differences we have here. And with all respect, I think all of us come here, lawyers, judges, and everyone else, and we have to adjust to the way the business is done here, hopefully rightly and fairly, and with due regard to the rights of the accused, which the Prosecution certainly supports and shouldn't be viewed as otherwise. It was, Your Honour -- Judge Clark, you were right. It was initially -- those documents, 17 binders, were initially provided to the Chamber and to the Defence as essentially advance disclosure, if I can put it that way, of the exhibits which we would tender at trial. It has always been our intention. And if I was not as clear on that as I should have been, then I apologise. It has always been our intention to tender the vast majority of those documents into evidence. But what we did indicate at the beginning of the trial was rather than tender them as we went, literally day by day, which it is our position we would have been entitled to do under the regime of this Tribunal, and the fact the Defence had not made a request for advance disclosure of documents, we didn't do that. We thought that would slow down the trial, undoubtedly raise complaints by the Defence that they had not seen the documents before. So to address those concerns, we provided these binders to everyone before the trial began. It is our intent, and we're moving in the direction of tendering most of those documents and exhibits. I agree with Your Honour that the terminology we use sometimes is not precise. They were provided to the Court and counsel initially, if you will, as a matter of disclosure - "proffer," as you say might be a more neutral word - but they were provided as disclosure. As the trial has progressed, I guess the next stage -- second step is to tender, offer - where I come from, we would probably say "offer" - the exhibits to the Chamber as evidence. We are now at a point where there is a substantial number of the documents, and 17 binders, I think, have been tendered or offered to the Court. More will be. And of course, then it is up to the Chamber to rule on the admission of the exhibits. I hope that answers your questions, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you saying then, Mr. Scott, that these 17 binders will be the source from which you will extract the documents which will then become exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would say, Your Honour, that they are the source of probably 90 per cent plus of the exhibits that we will tender in the course of our trial. The reason I qualify that, again to be perfectly transparent, is that there have indeed been some additional documents that have come to our attention since the trial began, a document that a witness brings with them to The Hague that we've never seen before. A document comes to us still from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So we are tendering those as we go. So I do not want to misunderstand -- anyone to misunderstand that every exhibit we have tendered was in those 17 binders before we began. There are a few exceptions, but I would say they're rather limited. So most are coming from the 17 binders. So think that part answers your question. The second part is, yes, it is our intention to offer the vast majority, and again I would say more than 90 per cent of the documents in those 17 binders, as exhibits. And in fact, I think we are very substantially on the way to doing that with the testimony of Mr. Van Hecke, with the testimony of Mr. Prlic. And we're going to tender a witness today on the international armed conflict binders, which is two binders, and we may in fact call another witness before the end of the week to tender additional collections of documents. There are also on our exhibit lists a substantial number of exhibits which were admitted in other cases in connection with the transcripts of testimony that the Chamber -- this Chamber has admitted from the other cases. There are approximately now, I think, about ten transcripts from either the Blaskic case or the Kordic case which this Chamber has ruled -- has admitted. They stand admitted. Not tendered, admitted. With those testimonies come a large number of exhibits. For instance, a senior ECMM official, Mr. Brix Andersen, testified in the Kordic case, and with his testimony went something like, off the top of my head, probably at least 80 ECMM documents, ECMM reports. Those have all been admitted. They were admitted when the Court ruled on his transcript. That's 80 ECMM documents right there. So there are a substantial number of documents. That's why I-- excuse me. That's why I say to the Chamber that if an accounting is made, a very substantial majority of the document in the 17 binders have in fact been tendered at this date. And again I respectfully submit that by hopefully in the next few days even more will be tendered. So we are well on our way to having tendered the vast majority of the 17 binders of documents and that is our intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Will there be any significant numbers of documents in the 17 binders which will not be dealt with by a witness? Apart from the ones on which there's been a legal ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There may -- yes. There will be some -- when you say "witness," there will and witnesses, for instance, a witness like Mr. Prlic, who tenders a collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. He gave us the provenance --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: -- and how the documents were put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They will not -- I would not want to mislead the Chamber to say that there will be a large number of individual fact witnesses, if I can use that terminology, through which all these exhibits will be tendered. The reality is on that point, if I can -- if this addresses part of your concern, Judge Clark, perhaps it doesn't, but I'll -- it may, the reality is, Your Honour, that many of these HVO documents, for instance, were of course prepared by HVO soldiers and officers and junior officers who prepared these kinds of documents. Candidly, those witnesses are not available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You may not be suggesting that, but that's the realities and again why the practices of this Tribunal differ from many national systems. Frankly, we do not have the same tools here. I come from a system where I have vastly and superior and more forceful tools to obtain evidence, in the United States, as Mr. Meek will be familiar with. I have do not have those tools available to me here. I cannot obtain the presence of a number of these witnesses. They simply will not come. And if they come, in all respect, I wouldn't -- I'll leave it at that. That's all we can do, Your Honour. But, yes, we are going to tender virtually all the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I really wanted to know, Mr. Scott, was will there be a bundle of documents which remain unaccounted for, where the provenance and the nexus to the case is not indicated by oral testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That is my major concern, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. I believe, Your Honour -- and if we fail to do so, it's because we tried and failed. But our effort will be to provide some provenance as to every document that's tendered to the Chamber in the way that we have been attempting to do. So it's not just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: A temporal nexus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The -- I'm sure what -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't know what you mean by that, a temporal nexus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In other words, that those documents relate to the events in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Oh, of course. Yes. Well, I think on those, many of them, of course, will speak -- as we've been hearing for the last couple of days, will speak for themselves. If you have an HVO document that reports on an attack on the 17th of April, 1993, and the provenance of the document has already been -- has been shown, then I would submit that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document, on its face, is at least relevant, and the Chamber will have to give it what weight it determines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I feel reassured greatly by what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank, Your Honour. I hope I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that this can turn into a kind of procedure debate on certain issues, but I will give you the floor, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Judge Clark, for asking this question, because the system I come from, "tender" we do use. We ask that an item or exhibit be admitted into evidence. So when this trial started, I was under a little bit of confusion, like Judge Clark was, as to what the Prosecution was doing tendering -- what he meant by "tendering." Then I believe that the tendering was, just as Mr. Scott said, that they would be available, and as witnesses came to testify, then when the foundation was laid, or proper foundation as far as this Prosecutor believed, then they would ask for admission of those documents. And I'm glad Judge Clark brought this question up. Am I to understand then that when this Prosecution tenders these documents he's asking that they be admitted at that moment, or is he just saying they're tendered now but at a later stage, after we have foundational evidence that we believe sufficient, we'll ask for the admission of the document or documents? I just want to be clear, and I think maybe that's one of the reasons I earlier filed for a Status Conference and got denied, but -- and I don't want to take up the Court's time today, but is that correct? Am I correct in that assessment? That's all I need to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there's one thing I would like to correct you, that you said that a Status Conference motion has been denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we're inviting both parties to submit to us a list of what you are going to talk about during our procedure meeting, because the procedure meeting, we are still waiting for the response from both parties. It seems to me the debate we are having now should fit in that procedure meeting rather than the real trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise. Initially, initially denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents the Defence counsel is going to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would ask that D1/32 be admitted -- tendered and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is this document going to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, so this document has been admitted. We will have about -- yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I would like leave to ask a procedural question very briefly, as I'm afraid I will not have another chance to do so. It has to do with the way in which witnesses are being examined. My question is linked to the method of direct examination of witnesses with respect to events that are not covered by the indictment. We have had two different situations in that regard. If I understood correctly the position of the Chamber, when Witness HH was being examined, the Prosecutor was not allowed to question the witness about events outside the scope of the indictment. However, when it came to Witness II, the witness was allowed to comment on events which were outside the scope of the indictment, but the Chamber said that they would judge what weight they would give to that part of the testimony. I should like to ask the Chamber if they would be so kind as to tell us what their position is. Is it the position of the Chamber that the Prosecutor in the examination-in-chief has no right to examine the witness about events which are not within the scope of the indictment. If that were so, then we would avoid repeated objections on those grounds. So as not to waste any more time, could you please assist me so that we can be guided by your advice, and we can avoid objections along those lines. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt you. I apologise. Your Honour, I think this issue, I suspect, is going to be more than a two-minute issue, and we would want to make a full response to this because we do have our own concerns about this. However, I must advise the Chamber, and I do think the document discussion - for me at least - has been helpful. I have a witness that can only testify today, and if we do not finish him this afternoon, he will not be in the Hague the next two days. And respectfully, I agree with Mr. Par, that we must have this discussion apparently, but if we could proceed with the witnesses and then postpone that discussion, Mr. President, I would greatly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is just what I want to say at this moment. I think the subject brought up by Mr. Par should be also a subject which should be dealt with during the procedural meetings or administrative meetings at a later stage. We need to have some equipment installed for the next witness. So we will have a break about ten minutes. We will resume at 10.30. --- Break taken at 10.17 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please remember that you are still under the solemn declaration. Now the cross-examination. Could we give the floor to Mr. Seric this time first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for this privilege. Cross-examined by Mr. Seric:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am counsel Branko Seric, and I am counsel for the accused Vinko Martinovic. When you think back to all the events in 1993 that you spoke about in your testimony, could we agree that you arrived at the Heliodrom on the 21st of July; then after three days you went to Bakina Luka to work, and then after that, they brought you to Vinko Martinovic to work on the 24th of July. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your mic ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they were put up at the headquarters near Rondo. Do you remember which was the vehicle that you were brought to and from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue vehicle, a blue truck. Was it Deutz or FAP, I wouldn't know the make exactly, but it was blue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the size of it? Was it a truck or a van? Was it open or closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: An open truck with -- an open truck, medium sized, not too big, about -- not more than 10 tonnes, but it was much larger than a van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of you would board it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty to thirty men. It varied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you sit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sat in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who came to fetch you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dinko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, was that organised, I mean this whole procedure about your travelling to and from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our names were taken down whenever we left the Heliodrom and whenever we returned from the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the building which housed the commander of the Mrmak ATG.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a cellar there, and there was the ground floor and one -- and the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many rooms were there in the cellar on the ground floor or on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cellar, I'm aware -- that is, I'm sure about two rooms down there. On the ground floor, three, and the WC; and on the upper floor, there was an ante room that I'm aware of, that I know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how high were the windows on the ground floor, I mean above the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 80 centimetres, metre from the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the surroundings of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were higher, because one could also see the cellar windows, so let's say about 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the surroundings of the building? Was it a building standing by itself, or were there some other buildings around it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you enter the building, to the left of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, to the left from the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a building standing on its own, or was it part of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a part of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please pause between question and answer. I don't have time to switch off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did Vinko Martinovic own a coffee bar nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were you personally taken to work and taken from work every day, that is, taken out in the morning and brought back in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that you spent the night in the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, a couple of nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us where you slept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you describe that room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rather large room from which -- in which a few of us slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any beds, furniture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two sofas in that room. I slept in a sleeping bag on a sponge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you use the toilet which was there on the floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rather, as a matter of fact, I'm not sure there were any such facilities on the first floor, but I could normally use the other toilet, and I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your movements around the building restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in daytime?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at night I did not move around because I was in that room, and in daytime, I moved around the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you go to the toilet whenever? Please wait until I finish and switch off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any guards either in the passages or in rooms or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was usually somebody in front of the building. No, there were none in the passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had full freedom of movement, and you could use everything that was in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these rooms inside, that's true, but I didn't quite understand what you are driving at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you once brought some hand grenades in. Does that mean that you also handled normally ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only once brought them from the vehicle, which -- into the building, that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have other weapons handy, within your reach?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, hardly. Well, I could see weapons, but there were always other people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those weapons guarded in any special way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they there would be a rifle or two belonging to men who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, you did anyone supervise and guard you all the time, in the morning, day, night, 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Vinko Martinovic offer you a flat in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into a private session for one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise this place on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now take the pointer, please, and show where were you exactly? Because you drew something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would come to this corner here. I would also go here. This here was all blocked with sandbags or bags filled with earth, across this street here. Then I also went to the health centre, and I'd come to the corner of this building. And I also went to this -- it could be this house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point exactly the direction of your movements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be coming from here, then moving here. Then we would walk through the health centre, down its passages to the end of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you took that route, were you ever exposed to any possible fire from the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only when we would be passing by the windows like the soldiers, like, for instance, the HVO soldiers who escorted us, and they also would double down passing by the windows as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you personally have to do often such occasions when you came there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repair, rather, to refill the sandbags; if they were damaged, try to repair that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point on this photograph, where was the separation line and where were the firing positions of the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side. No, I wouldn't know exactly where because I was never there. On the other side from the Bulevar, whether it was the first building or some buildings behind it, I was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, let's go back to the position where you say were the sandbags. How tall was this barricade, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, how tall it was, there were bags piled up. How tall? A metre and a half perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you think of yourself, did it reach up to your chest or above your head or?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't remember. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was of a certain height. If you bent down, you could see across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a cord above the sandbags with some blankets or sheets to serve as a kind of a screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't want to answer any questions that I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you allow for such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, because there were such cases elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. It seems to me that counsel is inviting the witness now to speculate as to whether a screen or blankets were in the area. He said that he doesn't know and that he wouldn't want to guess about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, the question you asked is not that proper, because you said, "Would you allow for such a possibility"? That's a speculation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever anywhere see that kind of thing, that there was a barricade with a cord, and then sheets or blankets or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I saw it at Podhum -- no, not at Podhum, above the upper part of Podhum later on when I went to work there. I know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you came to this place which you pointed next to the Health Centre, you say you don't remember if there were any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have some problems with the French interpretation, because we don't get it through the right channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's too fast. They are far in advance of the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, you have to make a pause after your question. And also, I have to tell the witness that maybe you're not familiar with the equipment in this courtroom. When you see the lights on the mic before the Defence counsel turned off, you begin to answer the question. It seems it's time for a break. We are adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness II, you have a marker somewhere there, please, to draw something for us, and I will give you a clean copy. Could the usher give the witness a clean copy of this for him to make some markings on it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark with the marker where those sandbags that you mentioned a moment ago were situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also please mark with a dotted line your route to reach the point where you told us you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the ELMO, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked copy will be given the number D1/33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That marked copy should be D2. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that D2/33?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am attorney Kresimir Krsnik, Defence counsel for Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please to meet you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've couple of very brief questions for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough and tell me, who guarded you at the Heliodrom? You were provided security at the Heliodrom? Please watch my microphone. Start with your answer when my light goes off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do that. They had white belts. They were military policemen who were there at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were responsible for you, for guarding you and everything that had to do with you who were there in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard testimony here, and in one of your prior statements, I don't want to refer you to it, but you said that you could take a shower at the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said you had two or three meals. Could you tell us now how many meals you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The quantities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. A loaf of bread. A normal loaf of 750 grams would be cut up into a half, then quarters. So one-quarter had to be taken twice. And then in the morning we would get tea or coffee with milk in containers from the UNHCR, and during the daytime we would get beans and then some pasta, macaroni, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please tell us, who guarded you in Dretelj? Who was responsible for that camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, people wearing white belts. I didn't know any one of the guards. The only person -- the only person I know was the commander who introduced himself when he interrogated us, and his name was Mr. Anicic. I never saw him before or since. He just said that he was Anicic, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. Most sincerely. And I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination? Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have two areas that I would like to ask you about very briefly. The first is when Ernest Takac threw you out of that window, was the window open or closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't closed as it was the kitchen. I've already said that the window was about a metre high when I entered the kitchen. Maybe you took my statement literally that he threw me out the window. But he hit me against the wall, and the window was up to the level of my hips. And then I would hit the roof of the garage with my back, and I would be thrown back and forth, and Ernest hit me like that a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then also, you testified that you felt in some ways safer at this place which was Stela's headquarters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that I felt safer because I went to Santiceva Street, to Bakina Luka. I was in the 9th battalion in Jasenica, in the 4th Battalion at Podhum where many people got killed. And in Santiceva, in fact, two people were shot in the crossfire between the BH army and HVO so that in the command, I didn't fear for my life as I did when my hand Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was injured and everything else, with the exception of that incident that I have described. I'm referring to the incident with Mr. Takac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you no longer go to the Stela headquarters after about two months and ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: My hand was injured. I went to Santiceva one day. My hand was injured. And after that, when this team, this group, had left, the four of them dressed in uniforms and with wooden rifles, I was afraid. And I did my best not to go anywhere. I hid, and I bandaged my hand. And I tried to conceal myself to avoid being sent to do labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have a few questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You told us a few days ago when you started to give your evidence that you and other Bosnian members of the HVO were arrested, I think. You said there were about 120 of you. Were you given any reason for why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they told us that Trijebanj where we were arrested, when the colleagues came to take over our shift, they just said that we would be interrogated. And if we were found to have no connections with the BH army, we would be released. But nobody asked me personally whether I was in the army. And when I saw that civilians were going with us to Dretelj, and when I found the other civilians there, then it became clear to me that the aim was not to establish whether I had anything to do with the army; it was simply my faith. Because large-scale conflicts had started on both sides, and the third side, that nothing could stop. And that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I really wanted to know was that were you satisfied that it was merely because of your faith that you were deprived of your liberty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I found myself with people who were 65 and 70 and children of 15 who never carried any weapons. Nobody interrogated me or asked me whether I was in the HVO and why I was not in the army and things like that, any other questions related to the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: As I understand your evidence, until the escape -- I may be wrong about this but this is how I understand it. Until the escape of 20 or so of your colleagues, the group of you who were in the HVO and who were Muslims were kept together at Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An entire unit was kept in the metal hangar, this unit of ours of 120. And then some others joined us when it was all over; that is, a couple of days after that, there were between 400 and 500 of us, or 450, both civilians and military men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Then we come to the excerpt from the Danish television video. Do you know the -- do you recall that being made or do you know the circumstances in which the Danish television team had access to the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was at the Heliodrom. I just heard that about two and a half months later they came for the prisoners, and they took them by truck to Split, and from there the prisoners were taken to Denmark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you were in -- I'm moving on now to the Heliodrom, when you had moved there. Did the men who were guarding you, who you believe were military police, did they know or were they made aware that all of you were formerly members of the HVO who had been detained or arrested because you were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't know at all which unit I belonged to, because no one asked me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was there any differentiation made between you and your colleagues who had been arrested while on duty with the HVO and other prisoners who were at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when it came to selecting people for work. The older people, the elderly, were not taken to work. As for everything else, there was no distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We've been hearing evidence from other witnesses from the Heliodrom who were -- who allege that they were tortured. Your evidence is that you were not maltreated, apart from the bad conditions under which you were detained and then the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one hurt me at the Heliodrom, me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How exactly were you injured? Were you caught in crossfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to my hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I was carrying a sandbag to -- in Santiceva Street, between the central prison, the main prison in Santiceva Street, and up there near the post office in the ERO Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At the time you were injured, were you taken in the truck from the Heliodrom to the Rondo or to the headquarters of the Mrmak before you moved down to Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time, I wasn't working for the Mrmak unit. It was another unit that had nothing to do with the Mrmak unit, as far as the location is concerned and everything else. I went back directly by truck from Santiceva Street to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: One final question. You were asked -- now I'm reading my own writing, which sometimes presents a problem. You were asked about a prisoner called [redacted]. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I didn't quite understand what your evidence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Judge Clark. I believe that this part of the witness's testimony was in private session for reasons which I can inform you about, but I would suggest that it would be appropriate to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My humblest apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Through the answers given to my colleague, I have received an answer to the first part of my questions. Now I come to the second group of questions. I heard the circumstances of the injury of your hand. I wanted to hear from you whether you were treated for that injury.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a soldier who was a doctor who bandaged my hand, and that was all. And then later, at the Heliodrom, again, there were two doctors, and they gave me some painkillers, because I had pain. And they changed the dressing. And this injury is still visible on my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of the Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one. Further re-examination by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the Heliodrom, were prisoners of war, that is Muslim members of the ABiH who were now prisoners, were they held in the same place, that is the same buildings, the same rooms, the same cells, if you know, with other Muslims who were civilians who were not members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the BH army who were captured before, they were in the central prison. They were not with me. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I wasn't going to go into Knez Domagoj Brigade matters, but I do have a couple of questions. Please watch the light on my microphone. Do you know, Witness, that members of the Knez Domagoj Brigade would arbitrarily leave their positions and would arbitrarily abandon their positions with the weapons and go over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from my unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would just object on the grounds that this question is beyond the scope of the questions put by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I also believe that your question is a little bit beyond the scope of the Judges' questions. This is not for another chance for the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there may be a misunderstanding. I'm talking about the unit that this gentleman belonged to, and Her Honour Judge Clark questioned him about that. Maybe the name confused you. It is the name of the brigade, but that is the unit that the witness was a member of, as he is confirming by nodding his head. And when the question was put to him why he was arrested, then it is fully in line with the questions posed by Her Honour Judge Clark. I apologise if there's any misunderstanding. I'm also interested in the reasons that brought about their arrest. That was a crucial question put by Her Honour. And for your benefit, Your Honours, I wanted to clear this point up, if I managed to do so with a couple of questions. Maybe it will make it clearer why the arrest took place. So my first question was whether this witness knows that Muslims belonging to the HVO, to that same brigade, would arbitrarily leave their positions fully armed and switch over to the BH army side. And then I'll also have a couple of other questions exclusively linked to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed. But just bear in mind that your questions should be closely related to the questions out of Judges' questions. And please lay a proper background for your question so that we know where you are leading us to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Witness, you have heard my question. So could you please answer it for me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that 120 of us were captured. A company has that number of men. I can't say with full responsibility, but out of my platoon that were -- that was on the line that day, no one was missing. Also in our unit, that unit, we had, more or less all of us, weapons which were our own weapons which we had purchased. So if something like that happened, it was not weapons that were taken from the HVO and taken to the BH army side because we had bought those weapons originally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that precisely when this arrest occurred, that Bijelo Polje, Sjeverni Logor were attacked and a major offensive launched by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, but I learned that after my arrest because I was never interested in politics. And I'm still not. I spent the whole night on the front line, on the front line in the bunker, so I had no idea as to what was happening. It was only later when I was arrested, my colleague that I had five or six drinks with on Tuesday in Capljina, and then I think it was Thursday that he came and was one of the group of men that arrested me. So I, as an individual. Again I'm speaking in my own name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your answer. And I appreciate the fact that you're always talking about what you know. Do you know that before the 30th of June, out of that whole brigade - that was my first question if you can answer it for me - there was arbitrary defection of people who would defect to the BH army? Not from your company but from the whole brigade. Do you know that from personal knowledge or did you perhaps know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I elaborate a little? We went to the front line for seven or 21. Later it was seven/seven, to Trijebanj. We would spend seven there and we would be seven off. So two units would go Trijebanj, and two units were composed exclusively of Muslims. The Croats, at the time, were off. So that front line from Hodovo to Rotimlje, you needed a lot of men to hold the front line. So I can't tell you out of those 250. I can't say that no one did, but the men who were near me from the platoon commander and the men in my unit, I can tell you that I personally really do not know of any individual who defected to the other side. Even -- I apologise for adding this. In fact, we were joined by a couple of other men, and one of them was my close relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't give us the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: A close relative from whom I learnt a lot and who was later killed at the separation line. And he joined this shift on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I understand. My final question: At the Heliodrom, in the premises in which you were held, the question of treatment was raised. Did all of you and the people you were able to see receive the same food, and were you served that food in the dining-room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all got the same food as far as the camp inmates were concerned, but it wasn't served in the dining-room. We left the hall, and in front there was a path leading to the sports field. Then one -- the persons held in one room would get out, form a line of two by two. Then the men distributing food would stand a couple of metres in front of the entrance. They would take the food and go inside, and then the other group would wait at the door for us to get in for them to go out, receive food, and go back in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this really is my last question: In front of the buildings that you were held - you call yourselves inmates. I agree - there were military policemen. Did they control who would go in and out? There weren't that many buildings. There were two or three buildings that constituted the prison. The rest of the buildings were occupied by the military or whoever. So these buildings were controlled by the military police who controlled people coming in and out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But may I -- may I say what I had to say? Yes, the police was there, and the police knew who was going where and what was happening when they went out, because there were cases when two men might be missing. They would take a couple of prisoners to make up for people they needed for a basketball team. So they may have been missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question. If someone took a prisoner to play basketball, even for that purpose the military police had to know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS II [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they also locked our door. The policemen would lock our door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. When the usher pulls the blinds down, he will take you out of the room. We all wish you good luck in your future. Thank you. At this stage --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution would tender first some photographs which were marked by the witness, Exhibit 21.8, Exhibit 20.8, Exhibit 11.18. Exhibit 14.4, I believe, is the one the witness made markings on during his testimony. Those are the photographs. In addition, we would tender the videotape footage of the Dretelj camp. And the only other exhibit referred to, I believe, Mr. President, was the part of Exhibit 704 on which the witness identified names of members of the -- of the ATG Mrmak. Mr. President, with your permission, I could add, and I hope it's okay for me to say this in response to one of Judge Clark's questions, there may be testimony previously given by a closed-session witness who was a member of a humanitarian organisation that might shed light on the time frame of the images which are shown in the Dretelj videotape. I believe there was testimony about the events shown in that videotape from the previous witness. It's a closed-session witness. I don't think I can mention the name at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there a number for that videotape? Is that P23?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, P23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is there a number for the witness so that I could look at the transcript and remind myself without disclosing his or her identity?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could -- I could give Your Honour the number that the witness has in the witness summaries which were filed. Oh, I'm sorry. Witness -- it's the third witness who testified in this trial. The third witness who testified in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections to those documents tendered by the Prosecutor? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as always when it comes to drawings, maps, and photographs whose origin is known, in all such cases, we do not have any objections, so that we have no objections to the exhibits offered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no, we do not object to these exhibits of the Prosecution, but the Defence should like to tender the document for which we have already been given the number. And that is D2/15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So the documents tendered by the Prosecutor through this witness have been admitted. And are there any objections concerning the documents tendered by the Defence counsel, namely, the D2/15?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be considered as admitted. And how about the next witness. Are you ready for the next witness, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if you will allow me to say something. We've fulfilled our plan -- and I think that the next witness is here. But we've fulfilled our plan with the witness; and if I may, I'd only like to take two minutes to address you which has to do with the discussion, with the debate initiated by Her Honour Judge Clark regarding the tendering of evidence. I have not had -- yet had the opportunity to say anything about it. I must say I am beginning to be very fearful and I am really beginning to be anxious about all this. I think it has to do with different legal systems and different decisions, and the Charter of the United Nations. And now I'm filled with fear, and I wanted to address you in a few sentences in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we have a witness waiting outside the room. I know that all of us are very interested in this issue. And this Trial Chamber has made a ruling that probably we'll have a special session for the procedural matters. We already informed both parties that we are expecting a list of the questions you are going to raise during that procedural meeting so that we could set the exact time for that. Would you please reserve your comments for that time. Thank you very much. Thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honours, the next witness is -- will be an open session witness. His name is Fransisco Aguirre, A-G-U-I-R-R-E. First name again, Fransisco. He is an OTP employee, and he will be testifying concerning some of the documents to be tendered, offered, by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I might say while he's coming in that it would be helpful to the Chamber and to counsel, and in fact perhaps more than helpful, if the two binders that have been previously provided and disclosed to the Defence some weeks ago concerning International Armed Conflict would be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could also make maximum use of our time -- we are trying to do that -- I tendered to the Chamber today -- some days ago the Chamber asked for a full version with the audio portion of the tape of the Vranica building. I think Judge Clark may have initiated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise. It has taken some time, for whatever reason, to put that together. But we do have it, and I will provide it to your staff at this time with one note. There is a middle portion -- the original tape was a compilation of I think at least two other cuts -- parts.
